comparison: Perfect agreement on C1-C4. Both evaluations find the molecular validation of the PTTH deletion mutant (genomic PCR, transcript analysis, protein immunoreactivity) to be well-supported with robust methodology and solid genetic evidence.
Perfect agreement on C5-C6. Both evaluations accept the developmental delay and increased body mass phenotypes as consistent with prior literature (Shimell et al., 2018) and not controversial.

Both support C7-C10 regarding the core behavioral phenotype. OpenEval finds the dose-dependent effect well-demonstrated. Peer reviewers acknowledge 'compelling data' but note inconsistency in heterozygote behavior across assays, questioning whether PTTH behaves as recessive or semi-dominant.

Divergent evaluations on C11-C12. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with caveat about technical limitations. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, noting 'limited scope of validation experiments' and that 'the inability to fully replicate the PTTHdelete phenotype through other means leaves some questions unanswered.'

Perfect agreement on C13. Both evaluations accept the genetic rescue experiment as part of solid genetic evidence, with no specific concerns raised about the rescue data despite OpenEval noting the ectopic expression caveat.

Both support C14-C16 anatomical characterization. OpenEval addresses C14-C16 specifically; peer review groups C14-C18 together, acknowledging the anatomical data and dsx expression without challenging the findings, though noting complexity in interpretation of biological significance.

Both support C17-C18 regarding PTTH-dsx co-expression. OpenEval finds strong evidence from double-labeling and intersectional genetics. Peer review acknowledges this as part of accepted anatomical characterization showing 'these neurons express the sex-determining gene dsx.'

OpenEval supports C19 (DsxF not required for receptivity regulation) as SUPPORTED. Peer review groups C19-C23 together as UNCERTAIN, raising concerns about control behavior in temporal inactivation experiments where one control 'behaves essentially the same as the experimental group.'

OpenEval supports C20-C21 (adult-stage activation shows no effect) as demonstrating temporal specificity. Peer review groups these with C19, C22-C23 as UNCERTAIN, acknowledging 'elegant data dissecting temporal requirements' but concerned about control behavior tempering conclusions.

OpenEval supports C22-C23 (larval stage critical period) as SUPPORTED with caveats about Gal80ts kinetics. Peer review includes these in UNCERTAIN evaluation, noting control behavior issues that weaken the temporal specificity conclusions.

Perfect agreement on C24-C27. Both evaluations support the stage 2 specificity findings, with peer reviewers acknowledging this demonstrates 'dual and temporally distinct role of PTTH/Ecdysone' and OpenEval noting systematic temporal activation with appropriate controls.

Perfect agreement on C28-C30. Both evaluations strongly support the ecdysone rescue experiment as compelling evidence. Peer reviewers consider this part of 'solid genetic evidence' and OpenEval notes appropriate vehicle controls demonstrating specificity.

OpenEval supports C31 (EcR expression in neurons) as SUPPORTED based on immunohistochemistry. Peer review groups C31 with C32-C37, accepting the receptor expression and downstream manipulations as part of evidence that 'Ecdysone, through its receptor EcR-A, is necessary during metamorphic neurodevelopment.'

Both support C32-C37 regarding receptor isoform and cell-type specificity. OpenEval provides detailed analysis of systematic dissection. Peer reviewers acknowledge the study 'identified the Ecdysone receptor and torso requirements of a particular subtype of pC1 neurons' with differential effects in pC1 vs vpoDN.

Perfect agreement on C38-C41. Both evaluations support the pC1b subtype identification through exclusion, with OpenEval noting the inference is based on exclusion rather than direct demonstration, and peer reviewers accepting this as part of identifying 'a particular subtype of pC1 neurons.'

Both support C42-C44 regarding behavioral consequences of EcR-A manipulation. OpenEval notes the distinction from true post-mating response. Peer reviewers acknowledge the data but comment on UAS-RNAi control effects on fertility that weren't discussed, though this doesn't challenge the data itself.

Divergent evaluations on C45-C46. OpenEval supports the pupal stage timing as SUPPORTED and consistent with earlier findings. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, noting that while panel J shows the effect, 'the behavior of one of the controls in panels I and K' matches the experimental group, making the conclusion 'too definitive.'

Both support C47-C50 regarding anatomical consequences of EcR-A knockdown. OpenEval notes all claims supported by imaging data with quantification. Peer reviewers acknowledge 'some effect on morphology is uncovered' and accept the morphological analysis as part of the evidence.

Both rate C51 with uncertainty. OpenEval explicitly marks as UNCERTAIN, noting the claim is speculative based on prior literature without direct connectivity evidence. Peer reviewers accept the morphological data but the speculative connectivity inference aligns with OpenEval's uncertainty.

Both support C52-C53. OpenEval notes calcium imaging clearly rules out activity changes, though connectivity inference is indirect. Peer reviewers provide 'convincing live calcium imaging showed no apparent effect of EcR-A in neural activity, although some effect on morphology is uncovered.'

Divergent evaluations on C54-C55. OpenEval supports the molecular feedback data as SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, viewing the feedforward explanation as 'insightful' but not fully resolving 'the initial confusion about the differing effects' between PTTH and ecdysone manipulations.

Divergent evaluations on C56-C57. OpenEval supports the anatomical observation as consistent with molecular data. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, noting the temporal mismatch: 'ptth is necessary during larval development, ecdysone effect appears during pupal development,' suggesting these may be 'independent processes.'

Divergent evaluations on C58-C61. OpenEval supports the torso data as SUPPORTED but notes 'direct' signaling claim is speculative. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, noting 'insufficient exploration of mechanistic pathways' and suggesting torso data indicates PTTH and ecdysone effects 'are independent of each other.'

Major divergence on C62-C66 main conclusions. OpenEval supports the integrated pathway model as SUPPORTED with caveats. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, with editor stating 'strength of the evidence is incomplete to support the main claim' and one reviewer concluding the pathways are 'more likely...independent processes' rather than PTTH regulating through ecdysone.

Both rate C67-C68 with uncertainty. OpenEval marks as UNCERTAIN, noting the 'general mechanism' claim is speculative and not directly tested. Peer reviewers challenge the 'SPECIFIC role' claim, noting metamorphic remodeling of entire CNS is likely altered, requiring examination of other behaviors before claiming specificity.
